newsitem.title: CHINA: China says concerned by trade surplus with U.S..
newsitem.headline: China says concerned by trade surplus with U.S..

text.p: A senior Chinese trade official said on Friday that China was concerned about its trade surplus with the United States and that it was encouraging domestic companies to step up imports from America.

But Washington needed to relax curbs on American technology exports and increase U.S. government export financing to reduce the trade gap, Sun Zhenyu, vice minister of foreign trade and economic cooperation, told reporters in Beijing.

"The (trade) issue has become such a general concern to the American people from all walks of life that failure to handle the issue properly could hold up the normal development of economic and trade relations between the two countries," Sun said in a statement delivered to reporters.
"We will continue to encourage our enterprises to expand imports from the United States," he said.
U.S. aircraft maker Boeing Co could be a beneficiary of the drive to buy American, he said.
He said he would not rule out the possible signing of large contracts, including a possible sale of Boeing aircraft to China, during the visit of U.S. Vice President Al Gore next week.
Sun added, however, that any contracts signings would depend on whether the companies involved reached agreement on acceptable terms. He did not give further details.

China on Friday also issued a white paper on its trade position with the United States giving its explanation of the trade imbalance, which has long been an irritant in Sino-U.S. ties already strained by a host of other disputes.
On Thursday, the United States said its deficit with China rose to $3.72 billion in January from $2.74 billion in January last year.

Sun said U.S. companies had lost out on major infrastructure contracts, particularly in the electric power sector, because of a lack of government financing, and he called for more support from the U.S. Export-Import Bank.
The trade official said Washington had blocked its own prospects in the nuclear power sector because of American restrictions on nuclear technology exports to China.
Sun noted that China had reduced import duties substantially in recent years and that further reductions would bring the average rate to 15 percent by the year 2000 from 23 percent now.
He said China was gradually reducing the number of items covered under import licences, saying that only 384 items required them now compared with more than 1,200 in the past.
He declined to say which ones might be removed from the licensing list in future but he said those remaining were generally related to weaker industries.
